summary:
Syria's Penal Code criminalises the conduct a trans visitor may be read as engaging in. Article 520 of the 1949 code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" and carries up to three years' imprisonment; Article 517 covers public indecency. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that both provisions are applied to women as well as men, so a trans visitor is reachable under the same articles irrespective of legal sex marker or presentation.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Syria, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. No anti-discrimination protection exists in any field. The state's response to same-sex conduct is criminalisation, which removes the complaint route a visitor would otherwise have after an assault, a refusal of service or a document dispute.

Enforcement has fallen on gatherings. In the weeks before 23 June 2010, Syrian authorities raided several private parties and arrested more than 25 men; most were charged with homosexual acts, others with drug offences, and charges also included encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Reporting from Damascus in October 2020 records that homosexuality and public decency offences are illegal there and quotes a 36-year-old describing meetings with friends in gay-friendly cafes as happening "only in whispers".

Violence against LGBTQ people, including beatings and torture, occurs frequently, and non-state armed actors are among the perpetrators. Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State have both attacked LGBTQ people, and the Islamic State executed people in areas under its control on accusations of sodomy.

Armed and political figures have endorsed harsher treatment rather than restraint. A Free Syrian Army member, Nasradeen Ahme, said he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while the secular figure Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would answer "no way" to gays claiming rights.

Official stigma reaches health care. In 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly described HIV/AIDS as divine punishment for fornication and homosexuality.

Organised social space for LGBTQ people has been eliminated. The region's only gay tour, running between Damascus and Aleppo, stopped operating, and the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus were eradicated. The Aleppo and Damascus hammams that hosted the pre-2011 tour, described by its organiser as a place where "we never had any problems", ended that activity with the civil war.
tangentialFactors:
The UN Security Council held its first discussion of LGBT concerns in August 2015, a closed session co-sponsored by the United States and Chile, at which two refugees from Syria and Iraq testified about constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and the Islamic State.

Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees face discrimination and exclusion in host countries on the basis of race, language, skin colour and religious background.
localsOnly:
For residents, legal gender recognition is impossible and there is no procedure to obtain it. LGBTI organisations cannot register, and no anti-discrimination protection applies in employment, housing, education or services.

The health system operates voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs and runs a limited HIV/AIDS education programme for youth in secondary schooling. Comprehensive public education aimed at LGBTQ people does not exist. The Health Ministry reported 369 infections, a figure NGOs estimated to be at least five times too low, and the UN criticised the government for ineffective prevention. Prevalence is low: under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1 per cent among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through the third quarter of 2019 since the first infections were recorded in 1987.

Digital expression continues anonymously. The "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020 and later moved to Twitter, with university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographing themselves by a faculty building under #oneofyou; most used fake accounts for fear of being identified. Reactions ranged from defence to threats of blood, and the activity faded amid COVID-19.
outOfScopeNotes:
A claim that LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs was investigated by Guardians of the Gem through its on-the-ground reporter network and found inaccurate; the organisation published the finding to avoid stirring incitement against the community.

Whether the authorities that took power in December 2024 have changed enforcement of Articles 520 and 517 is unresolved. No post-2024 prosecution record is available.

The European Union Agency for Asylum's Syria country focus material yielded no assessment of treatment by state, non-state or societal actors.
